why.correct: Nomadic herding fits dry grasslands too dry for crops. The letter in East Asia, A, marks Mongolia, where herders move animals to fresh grass with the seasons.
options: Right: A marks Mongolia, in East Asia, where nomadic herding on dry grasslands is common.
B marks Brazil. Its Amazon rainforest is better known for shifting cultivation, not herds moving across dry grassland.
C marks Malaysia, a hot, wet country known for oil palm plantations, not herding.
D marks Argentina. It has grasslands, but cattle there are mostly raised on fenced ranches that stay in one place.

why.correct: The farming described is shifting cultivation, an extensive system of tropical rainforests. The Amazon rainforest lies mostly in Brazil, marked B.
options: A marks Mongolia: its dry grasslands support herding, not cleared rainforest plots.
Right: B marks Brazil, and the Amazon rainforest is a region where shifting cultivation is practiced.
C marks Malaysia, which has rainforest (and some shifting cultivation on Borneo), but the Amazon is in South America, not Southeast Asia.
D marks Argentina, whose temperate grasslands (the Pampas) are used for ranching and grain, not rainforest plots.

why.correct: A compare speaks of both sides. Mongolia, marked A, and Argentina, marked D, both use huge areas with few inputs per hectare to raise livestock, so both are extensive. They differ in movement: nomadic herders move; ranchers raise animals on fixed land.
options: Tree crops on big estates describe plantation agriculture, as in Malaysia, not Mongolia or Argentina.
Herding in A uses very few inputs per hectare, so it is extensive, not intensive.
Clearing plots and letting them recover is shifting cultivation, found in rainforests such as Brazil's.
Right: both are extensive livestock systems; herders in Mongolia move with their animals, while ranchers in Argentina keep cattle on fixed, fenced land.

why.correct: The map shows C in Southeast Asia, near the equator. Oil palm estates in Malaysia are a plantation system: large, intensive, one crop, grown for sale far away.
options: Mediterranean agriculture needs dry summers and mild, wet winters, not the year-round heat and rain of Malaysia.
Right: a large estate growing one crop for export in a tropical country is plantation agriculture.
Market gardening grows many fruits and vegetables near the shoppers who buy them, not one tree crop for export.
Herding raises animals on dry grasslands; the estates in Malaysia grow a crop.

why.correct: Intensity is about inputs per unit of land, not farm size. Farm 1 puts the most money and labor into each hectare.
options: Farm 4 is the largest farm, but it spends only 20 dollars a hectare: large area with few inputs is extensive.
Farm 2 spends 500 dollars a hectare, far less than Farm 1.
Right: Farm 1 spends the most per hectare (4,000 dollars) and has the most workers on the smallest area.
Farm 3 spends 900 dollars a hectare, less than a quarter of Farm 1's spending.

why.correct: <math class="hug-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>000</mn></mrow><mn>4</mn></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>500</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{2{,}000}{4} = 500</annotation></semantics></math> hectares per worker. So few workers on so much land is a mark of extensive agriculture.
Read the table across. Output per hectare measures intensity, not success. Multiply it by area: Farm 4 produces 90 × 2,000 = 180,000 dollars, while Farm 1 produces 30,000 × 2 = 60,000 dollars.
options: Right: 90 dollars a hectare on 2,000 hectares is 180,000 dollars in all, more than any other farm's total. Extensive farms earn from area, not from each hectare.
Farm 4 has 4 workers, the same as Farm 3 and fewer than Farm 1.
Farm 4 spends 20 dollars a hectare, much less than Farm 2's 500 dollars.
The table does show it: 90 dollars a hectare.

why.correct: Intensive and extensive describe inputs (labor, money, machines, fertilizer) per unit of land.
options: Size alone does not decide it. Many very large farms, such as ranches, are extensive.
Right: intensive agriculture puts many inputs into each unit of land.
Where a crop is sold says nothing about the inputs used on each hectare.
Dairy farms near cities raise animals and are intensive; nomadic herds are extensive.

why.correct: Shifting cultivation, nomadic herding and ranching are the extensive systems: much land, few inputs per hectare.
options: Right: herders use huge areas of grassland with few inputs per hectare.
Right: cattle graze large fenced areas with little labor per hectare.
Greenhouse vegetables use much labor, heat and fertilizer on small plots: intensive.
Plantations use many workers and much money on each hectare: intensive.
Corn Belt farms put machines, seed and fertilizer into every hectare: intensive.

why.correct: Climate shapes what can be grown. All three places have a Mediterranean climate, and farmers there grow drought-tolerant tree and vine crops, often with irrigation in summer.
options: Year-round rain describes tropical climates, such as Malaysia's, which suit plantation crops.
Short summers rule out slow-ripening crops like olives and citrus.
Grassland too dry for crops supports herding or ranching, not orchards and vineyards.
Right: that is the Mediterranean climate, and the crops of Mediterranean agriculture can survive the summer drought.

why.correct: Irrigation is the human supply of water to crops. It lets dry places, such as the Imperial Valley in California, be farmed intensively, a sign of possibilism: people use technology to work around the environment.
options: Right: irrigation supplies the water rain does not, so farmers can put many inputs into each hectare.
Moving herds describes nomadic herding, an extensive use of dry land.
Long rest periods describe shifting cultivation and lower the use of each hectare.
The Imperial Valley gets very little rain; that is why it needs canals.

why.correct: Shifting cultivation works when the land has a long rest (it is left fallow). When more people need food from the same forest, the rest shrinks, the soil is worn out and yields fall: the land is pushed past its carrying capacity.
options: More frequent use without time to recover lowers yields on poor rainforest soils.
Herding needs open grassland, not rainforest.
Right: the long rest rebuilds nutrients; cutting it short wears out rainforest soils and yields drop.
Shortening the rest period changes the soil, not the regional climate.

why.correct: Market gardening (also called truck farming) is intensive and sits close to its market because its products are perishable and in high demand.
options: Land near cities usually costs more, which is one reason market gardens use it so intensively.
Market gardens grow in many climates; greenhouses even make their own.
Market gardening grows crops, not herds.
Right: perishable crops need a short trip to the people who buy them.

why.correct: Mixed crop and livestock farming, common in the US Corn Belt and much of Europe, links crops and animals on one farm. It is intensive.
options: Ranching grazes animals over large areas of grassland; it does not center on growing feed crops.
Right: crops and animals are raised together on one farm, and the crops feed the animals.
Plantations grow one crop, usually in the tropics, for sale far away.
Shifting cultivation moves from plot to plot in a forest.

why.correct: Climate shapes the pattern. The dry belt from the Sahara to the Gobi has too little rain for most crops, so herding animals that move to new grass is a way of using it.
options: Dry grasslands are among the cheapest land, which suits a system using so much of it.
Year-round heavy rain describes rainforests, used for shifting cultivation and plantations.
Right: where rain is too low and uncertain for crops, moving animals to grass is a way to farm the land.
Herds need huge areas, far from crowded places.

why.correct: A strong answer names a real place, the concept and the link: extensive means few inputs per unit of land.
Township and range divides land into a grid of squares, so fields and roads meet at right angles.
options: Right: panel 2 is a grid of equal squares with straight roads, the mark of township and range.
Panel 1 has odd-shaped fields that follow a stream and markers such as a tree and a rock: metes and bounds.
Panel 3 has long, narrow strips running back from a river: long lots.
Neither panel 1 nor panel 3 is a grid: look for the equal squares.

why.correct: The long lot system gave each family a narrow frontage on the river, the main road of the time, and a long strip running inland.
options: Panel 1 shows metes and bounds, used in colonies such as Virginia, not in French Quebec.
Panel 2 shows the US township and range grid.
Right: French settlers divided land into long lots, each with a narrow river front.
Neither has the long, narrow strips running from a river that French settlement left.

why.correct: Long lots gave every farm a share of the most valuable thing nearby, river access, which is also why the houses line up along the river.
options: Equal squares are the goal of township and range, panel 2.
Following natural features is metes and bounds, panel 1.
Roads at right angles mark the grid in panel 2.
Right: the river was the highway and water source, so each lot was cut to give every family a piece of riverbank.

why.correct: Metes and bounds describes land by distances and natural landmarks. It was the method of the eastern colonies, so their field patterns are irregular.
options: Kansas and Iowa were surveyed later with the township and range grid.
Right: metes and bounds was used in the original colonies and some states formed from them.
French settlement in Louisiana left long lots, panel 3.
Satellite surveying is not one of the three methods shown.

why.correct: The Land Ordinance set up the rectangular survey known as township and range.
options: Metes and bounds uses natural landmarks and irregular lines, not a planned grid of squares.
Long lots are narrow strips running back from a river, not squares.
Right: squares 6 miles on a side split into 36 one-square-mile sections is township and range.
Linear settlement is a pattern of houses along a line, not a survey method.

why.correct: <math class="hug-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>36</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>640</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>23</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>040</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">36 \times 640 = 23{,}040</annotation></semantics></math> acres in one township.
The survey method shaped the settlement pattern: square parcels sold to single families produced dispersed settlement across the Midwest.
options: Right: families bought their own section or part of one and built on it, so houses spread out across the grid.
Selling land in separate squares to separate families led people to live on their own land, not in villages.
A row of houses along a river fits long lots, not the square grid.
The land was sold to farmers who settled on it.

why.correct: Clustered settlement groups homes in a village and keeps farmland outside it.
options: Dispersed settlement scatters homes across the land, one on each farm.
Right: homes grouped together, with farmland around them, is clustered (nucleated) settlement.
Linear settlement lines homes along a road, river or shore.
Long lot is a survey method, not a settlement pattern.

why.correct: A linear settlement follows a line on the land: here, the Nile and its canals in the desert.
options: A square grid fits township and range, which leads to dispersed farms, not lines.
Most Egyptian farmers in the Nile valley live in fixed homes, not moving herds.
Hilltop villages for defense would be clustered and away from the water.
Right: the river and canals bring water to crops, so homes line up along them.

why.correct: Clustering trades a longer walk to the fields for shared water, safety, services and community.
options: Right: living close together makes it easier to share services and protect one another.
Living beside your own fields leads to dispersed settlement.
Separate squares sold to families led to dispersed farms in the US Midwest.
In a clustered village farmers walk farther to their fields: that is a cost of clustering.

why.correct: Survey methods divide land; settlement patterns describe where homes sit. The method a place used often shaped its pattern.
options: Right: the grid is visible from the air over much of the US Midwest.
Right: that is why its fields have irregular shapes.
Long lots were laid out by French settlers along rivers in places such as Quebec and Louisiana.
Homes grouped in a village is clustered settlement.
Linear settlement lines homes along a road, river or shore.

why.correct: The grid repeats across the Midwest and West, a regional pattern produced by a national survey system.
options: Farmers did not choose the lines; the national survey did, the same way across many states.
Long lots in Quebec and metes and bounds in Virginia show the grid is not everywhere.
Right: the grid covers a whole region of the country, and it comes from the US township and range survey.
River banks shape long lots, not a grid of straight roads.

why.correct: Survey methods leave a lasting mark. Colonial metes and bounds left irregular parcels in Virginia; the 1785 grid left squares across Iowa.
options: Virginia has a wet climate; the shapes come from how the land was first divided.
Iowa has mixed crop and livestock farming on fixed fields.
Long lots fit French settlement in Quebec and Louisiana, not Virginia.
Right: Virginia used metes and bounds in colonial times; Iowa was later surveyed by township and range.

why.correct: Metes and bounds relies on landmarks. When landmarks change, neighbors may disagree on where the line is: a known limit of the method.
options: A fixed square of one mile is a section in township and range, not metes and bounds.
Right: features that change or vanish make metes and bounds lines hard to find, which leads to disputes.
The deed puts the boundary at the creek, so the farm touches it.
The deed describes a boundary, not where houses stand.

why.correct: Dispersed and clustered settlement trade off differently: dispersed homes are close to the fields but far from services; clustered homes are the reverse.
options: That is a cost of clustered settlement: villagers walk out to their fields.
Kansas farms are large; dispersed homes sit on big parcels.
Right: with each home on its own farm, services are spread far apart.
Kansas was surveyed by township and range, a grid.

why.correct: Name the place, the method and the effect with its link (so): long lots put every house on the river, a linear pattern.
The Fertile Crescent arcs through Southwest Asia, from the eastern Mediterranean through the Tigris and Euphrates valleys. On this map it is A.
options: Right: A is in Southwest Asia, in the area of the Tigris and Euphrates rivers, part of the Fertile Crescent.
B marks the Indus River valley in South Asia, another early hearth.
C marks Central America, the hearth of maize, beans and squash.
E marks the Andes of South America, where potatoes were domesticated.

why.correct: Central America (often called Mesoamerica) is the hearth of maize, beans and squash. It is C on this map.
options: A is the Fertile Crescent, the hearth of wheat and barley.
Right: maize was domesticated in what is now southern Mexico, in Central America.
D is in Southeast Asia, a hearth of crops such as taro and rice.
E is the Andes, the hearth of the potato.

why.correct: Distance and the oceans were the barrier. Once ships linked the hemispheres, the Columbian Exchange spread crops between hearths that had developed separately.
options: Maize and potatoes were domesticated thousands of years before 1492.
Maize and potatoes now grow widely in Southwest and South Asia, so climate was not the barrier.
People in Southwest and South Asia traded widely; their trade simply did not reach the Americas.
Right: the Atlantic and Pacific kept the Americas' crops apart from Afro-Eurasia until ships crossed after 1492.

why.correct: The map shows several hearths with different crops: wheat in A, maize in C, potatoes in E. Each was domesticated from local wild species, a sign of independent invention.
options: Farming arose independently in several hearths, and spreading took thousands of years.
Right: there was no single origin; people in different regions domesticated their own local wild plants and animals.
Farming began at different times in different hearths.
There was no regular contact between the Americas and Asia before 1492.

why.correct: The Columbian Exchange moved plants, animals and diseases between the Americas and Afro-Eurasia after 1492. The potato is one of its best-known crops.
options: That is the first domestication of plants and animals, thousands of years earlier, in the Andes itself.
An ocean lies between them; the potato crossed it by ship.
Right: after 1492, ships carried crops such as the potato from the Americas to Europe.
The passage says the plant itself was carried to Europe.

why.correct: Depending on one crop is risky. When blight struck the one potato variety most poor families relied on, their main food source collapsed.
options: Right: when the one crop failed, those families had little else to eat.
The passage says the potato grew well in Ireland's climate.
It arrived in the late 1500s, more than 200 years earlier.
The passage does not say that; it says many Irish people later moved to the United States.

why.correct: A famine at home is a push factor. The passage links a farming event to a migration flow, a cross-unit link the exam often asks for.
options: A pull factor draws people to a destination; the famine pushed them from Ireland.
Right: the famine was a condition at the origin that drove people away.
An intervening opportunity is a chance found along the way that ends a move early.
Leaving Ireland for the United States is international migration.

why.correct: Domestication is the slow change of wild species into crops and livestock that depend on people, through people choosing which ones to plant or breed.
options: Moving plants between continents is diffusion, such as the Columbian Exchange.
That describes shifting cultivation.
That is irrigation.
Right: people kept seeds and animals with traits they wanted, and over many generations the species changed.

why.correct: Farming meant staying near fields and herds, and stored surpluses let villages grow. Permanent settlement followed.
options: Right: tending crops and storing food tied people to one place.
Farmers in Afro-Eurasia had no contact with the Americas at that time.
Tractors came thousands of years later.
Herding involves moving, the opposite of living in one place year-round.

why.correct: Farming in hearths like the Fertile Crescent made more food than farmers needed. That surplus supported larger populations, towns and people with other jobs.
options: Food surpluses supported larger, not smaller, populations.
Farming spread; it did not give way to herding.
Right: a surplus feeds people who make tools, trade, write or govern, so jobs became specialized.
Domesticated crops became the main food.

why.correct: The Columbian Exchange moved animals as well as plants. Horses from Europe spread across the Plains and changed hunting and travel.
options: That is the first domestication of local plants and animals thousands of years earlier.
Plains nations hunted wild bison; they did not domesticate them.
The horse itself was carried across the ocean, then spread across the land.
Right: the horse came from Afro-Eurasia and transformed how Plains nations hunted and traveled.

why.correct: Maize, potatoes, tomatoes, cacao and cassava went from the Americas to Afro-Eurasia. Wheat, rice, sugarcane, coffee, cattle and horses went the other way.
options: Right: domesticated in Central America, now grown on every inhabited continent.
Right: from the Andes of South America.
Wheat came from the Fertile Crescent and went the other way, to the Americas.
Sugarcane came from Asia and was carried to the Americas.
Coffee came from the highlands of Ethiopia in Africa.

why.correct: Domestication came about 10,000 years ago; the Columbian Exchange began in 1492; the potato spread in Ireland over the next two centuries; the blight struck from 1845.
Farming spread outward from its hearth to neighboring areas, which is expansion diffusion (contagious). The Columbian Exchange, by contrast, carried crops across an ocean: relocation diffusion.
options: Relocation diffusion moves an idea with people to a distant place; here farming crept outward step by step.
Right: farming spread outward from its hearth while staying strong at home, a form of contagious expansion diffusion.
Cities did not yet exist across Europe; farming spread through neighboring lands.
The same crops and practices spread, not just an idea that was changed.

why.correct: A full answer names the item, the place and the effect, joined by "so".
Read each column from top to bottom: farming's share of workers falls, food per farm worker rises and the share of people in towns rises.
options: Right: food per farm worker rose from 100 to 320 while the share in farming fell from 75% to 25%.
Both parts are reversed: food per worker rose and the share in farming fell.
The share in towns rose, from 15% to 60%.
It fell by 50 percentage points, from 75% to 25%.

why.correct: <math class="hug-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>320</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>100</mn></mrow><mn>100</mn></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mn>100</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{320 - 100}{100} \times 100</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="hug-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mn>220</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= 220\%</annotation></semantics></math>.
This is the Second Agricultural Revolution's key effect: more food from fewer farmers freed labor for town and factory work.
options: The table shows towns growing, not shrinking.
Food per farm worker rose, not fell.
Right: as each worker grew more food, farms needed fewer hands, and people moved to towns to work, often in factories.
Food per farm worker rose sharply; the table shows no shortage.

why.correct: A national table summarizes the whole country. Some regions may have mechanized early and others late; data at a smaller scale would be needed to see that.
options: It does: the second column.
It shows four years, from 1750 to 1900.
It shows three different measures.
Right: the table is at the national scale, so it cannot show which regions changed fastest.

why.correct: Mechanization means replacing human and animal labor with machines, a core part of the Second Agricultural Revolution.
options: Domestication changes wild plants and animals into crops and livestock; the reaper is a machine.
Right: a machine took over work that people had done by hand.
Shifting cultivation is clearing forest plots in turn, not using machines.
The Columbian Exchange moved crops and animals between hemispheres.

why.correct: The reaper raised output per worker at harvest time. It saved labor rather than growing more grain on each acre.
options: The passage is about harvesting, not water.
The reaper was pulled by horses.
Right: the passage says a few people could harvest many times more land in a day.
The reaper made cutting faster; it did not change how much grain grew on an acre.

why.correct: Fewer farm jobs pushed people off the land, while factory jobs pulled them to towns: farming change and migration are linked.
options: Right: labor-saving machines meant fewer jobs on farms, a push toward towns and factories.
Machines reduced the number of hands needed.
Nothing in the change pushed families to the tropics.
Reapers made wheat cheaper to harvest, so wheat spread.

why.correct: The Second Agricultural Revolution began in Britain and western Europe in the 1700s, alongside the rise of factories, and spread to North America in the 1800s.
options: That is the First Agricultural Revolution.
Right: new rotations, breeding and tools spread there from the 1700s, then to North America in the 1800s.
Later changes to grain farming in South Asia and Mexico came in the 1960s; the Second Agricultural Revolution was much earlier.
The Andes was a hearth of the potato, not of this revolution.

why.correct: Rotating wheat, turnips, barley and clover kept every field busy and fed animals through winter. Clover added nitrogen, a nutrient wheat needs.
options: Clover was mostly grazed by farm animals, not sold abroad.
Wheat, barley and turnips grew there too.
Its main jobs were feed and restoring nitrogen to the soil.
Right: clover fed livestock and restored the soil, so no field had to lie empty.

why.correct: Better feed meant larger herds and better diets, one reason people in Britain grew healthier and lived longer.
options: Right: more animals kept through winter meant more meat and dairy.
Feed crops let farmers keep more animals, not fewer.
Animal foods increased.
Rotation protected the soil and raised output.

why.correct: Linking units: more and better food lowers death rates; as farms need fewer hands and families move to towns, birth rates later fall. Real countries only roughly fit the model.
options: More food lowered death rates; the diseases of the Columbian Exchange hit the Americas hardest.
It cut farm jobs, which over time lowered the value of large families.
Right: more food cut deaths (stage 2); later, town life and less need for child labor on farms helped birth rates fall (stage 3).
It pushed many people from rural areas to towns.

why.correct: Enclosure had positive and negative effects: more productive farms, and also landless families who moved to towns for work.
options: Strips from rivers are long lots, a French survey method in North America.
Enclosure ended shared use of the commons; it did not bring back foraging.
Square sections are part of the US township and range survey.
Right: enclosure allowed new rotations and breeding on larger farms, and it pushed many rural families off the land.

why.correct: The Second Agricultural Revolution brought new rotations, selective breeding, enclosure and machines, first in Britain and then in North America.
options: Right: the Norfolk four-field rotation spread in the 1700s.
Right: mechanization was central to it.
That happened thousands of years earlier, in the First Agricultural Revolution.
That is shifting cultivation, an old extensive system.
That was the Columbian Exchange, after 1492.

why.correct: About 10,000 years ago; the late 1500s; the 1700s; the 1850s.
Place, cause and effect joined by "so": the link between mechanization and migration to towns.
A compare speaks of both lines: both rise, but the irrigated plain pulls far ahead after 1960, when Green Revolution seeds spread.
options: Right: Region X climbs from 1.0 to 2.8 after 1960, while Region Y rises slowly to 1.2.
Region X rises steeply; Region Y rises slowly. Neither falls.
In 2000 Region X yields 2.8 and Region Y 1.2 tonnes per hectare.
Both lines rise, Region X much more steeply.

why.correct: <math class="hug-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>2.5</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>1.0</mn></mrow><mn>1.0</mn></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mn>100</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{2.5 - 1.0}{1.0} \times 100</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="hug-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mn>150</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= 150\%</annotation></semantics></math>.
The Green Revolution was a package: high-yield seeds plus irrigation, fertilizer and pesticides. Where water was short, yields rose much less.
options: If Region Y had planted them first, its line would rise first; it rises least.
The legend calls Region X an irrigated plain.
Right: high-yield varieties give big gains only with irrigation and fertilizer, which the irrigated plain had.
GMOs spread on farms from the late 1990s, not the 1960s.

why.correct: Results at one place do not show a global pattern. Regions without irrigation, such as much of Sub-Saharan Africa, gained far less.
options: Region X keeps rising, from 2.5 to 2.8.
It starts in 1950.
Region Y rose more slowly.
Right: the chart itself shows uneven results; one region cannot stand for the world.

why.correct: Wheat breeding in Mexico from the 1940s and 1950s gave the seeds that South Asian farmers later adopted.
options: A marks India, which later planted the Mexican wheat widely from the mid-1960s.
Right: B marks Mexico, where the new wheat varieties were bred.
C marks the Philippines, where a rice institute bred the high-yield rice IR8.
D marks Niger, in the dry Sahel of West Africa.

why.correct: IR8 came from the International Rice Research Institute in the Philippines and spread across rice-growing Asia.
options: A marks India, a major adopter of the new rice and wheat.
B marks Mexico, where the wheat was bred.
Right: C marks the Philippines, home of the International Rice Research Institute.
D marks Niger, where rice is a minor crop.

why.correct: The Green Revolution centered on wheat and rice with irrigation. Dry regions growing millet, sorghum and cassava, such as the Sahel, gained less.
options: Right: the new seeds were mainly wheat and rice and needed water, which much of Niger lacks.
Niger has been farmed for thousands of years; its farmers grow millet and sorghum.
Niger is closer to the equator than India; the limits are water and crop type, not latitude.
GMO crops did not spread on farms until the late 1990s.

why.correct: The term was coined in 1968, and the main spread ran from the 1960s into the 1980s.
options: That was the Second Agricultural Revolution.
Right: the new seeds spread widely from the mid-1960s through the 1980s.
That was the First Agricultural Revolution.
GMO crops came into wide use from the late 1990s, after the Green Revolution.

why.correct: High-yield varieties were bred by crossing plants, not by lab gene changes. Short, stiff stalks held heavier grain, and yields depended on water and fertilizer.
options: That describes a GMO. Green Revolution seeds came from careful cross-breeding.
It needs more of both to reach its high yields.
Many were bred short, so heavy heads of grain would not knock the stalks over.
Right: high-yield varieties were bred to turn water and fertilizer into more grain.

why.correct: Keep the two apart: Green Revolution seeds were bred by crossing plants (1960s to 1980s); GMOs have genes changed in a lab and spread from the late 1990s.
options: Right: the Green Revolution used cross-bred seeds from the 1960s; lab gene changes spread on farms from the late 1990s.
GMOs came after the Green Revolution, not before.
Soybeans were domesticated in East Asia; in any case, this is not why the claim is wrong.
New high-yield seeds were at its center.

why.correct: Irrigated rice and wheat need much water. Pumping more groundwater than rain replaces makes water tables fall, a cost of the package.
options: Punjab's land is intensively farmed, not returning to forest.
Green Revolution farming uses more fertilizer, not less.
Right: heavy pumping for thirsty crops has lowered groundwater levels in Punjab.
The problem comes from pumping, not from changes in rain.

why.correct: The package favored farmers with land, water and credit. Inequality between farmers often grew even as total food supply rose.
options: Harvests grew, and grain prices generally fell.
Green Revolution farming is intensive and fixed.
More grain made rice and wheat more widely available.
Right: seeds, fertilizer, pumps and pesticides cost money, so larger farmers gained most and some small farmers borrowed heavily.

why.correct: Malthus (1798) argued food grows slowly. The Green Revolution raised yields so much that food per person rose in many countries. Neo-Malthusians reply that it depends on water and fuel that may run short.
options: That is Malthus's claim; the Green Revolution is evidence against it.
Right: Malthus expected food supply to grow slowly; new seeds and inputs made it grow quickly.
Population kept growing; food grew faster.
Malthus linked famines to too many people for the food; the Green Revolution showed food supply can rise.

why.correct: High-yield seeds, fertilizer, irrigation, pesticides and machines made up the Green Revolution package.
options: Right: the core of the package.
Right: the new seeds needed both to reach high yields.
GMOs came in the late 1990s, after the Green Revolution.
That was part of the Second Agricultural Revolution in the 1700s.
That is shifting cultivation, an extensive system.

why.correct: The First Agricultural Revolution, the Second (1700s to 1800s), the Green Revolution (1960s to 1980s), then GMO crops (late 1990s).
Place, technology and effect, joined by "so".
Read up from 10 km on the distance axis: the market gardening line is highest, so that use would outbid the others for this land.
options: Right: at 10 km market gardening can pay about 700 dollars a hectare, more than grain or ranching.
Grain can pay about 340 dollars a hectare at 10 km, less than market gardening.
